prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. Individualized Damages Questions Overwhelm Any Common Questions, Defeating Predominance Under Rule 23(b)(3).

A class may be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving predominance by a preponderance of the evidence, and the court must conduct a "rigorous analysis" and resolve the factual and legal disputes relevant to certification, even where they overlap with the merits. *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 675–76 (7th Cir. 2001); *see also Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). That inquiry requires the court to weigh the common questions against the individual ones, not merely to count the common questions. *See Kleen Prods. LLC v. Int'l Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 925–26 (7th Cir. 2016). The question is whether adjudicating the common issues will meaningfully advance resolution of the case, or whether the real work lies in individualized proceedings.

### A. Damages Are Not Merely Residual Here.

Defendant recognizes that this Court has held that the need for individualized damages calculations does not, standing alone, defeat certification. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013); *Bell v. PNC Bank, N.A.*, 800 F.3d 360, 380 (7th Cir. 2015). But that principle assumes that liability and injury can be established on a classwide basis and that what remains is a mechanical computation. It has no application where, as here, the individualized inquiry goes to whether and how each class member was harmed, and to the measure of that harm. Where "the individual questions are the heart of the case," predominance is absent. *See Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815–17 (affirming denial of certification where individualized proof was needed to show that each class member was injured and to establish the amount of any damages).

Here, Plaintiffs' damages theory requires the factfinder to determine, member by member, [describe individualized variables, e.g., the price each member paid, the value each received, whether and when each suffered a loss, and any offsetting benefit]. These are not arithmetic exercises. Each depends on testimony and documents unique to each class member and would require thousands of mini-trials. A class that must be "decertified" into individual proceedings at the damages phase was never manageable to begin with.

### B. Plaintiffs' Damages Model Does Not Fit Their Liability Theory.

Even where individualized damages questions are not dispositive, a plaintiff must show that damages are capable of measurement on a classwide basis and that the model matches the theory of liability. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34–35 (2013). Plaintiffs' proposed methodology fails that test. It [assumes a uniform injury / averages across heterogeneous members / does not isolate damages attributable to the theory of liability]. A model that cannot distinguish injured from uninjured members, or loss caused by the alleged conduct from loss caused by other factors, cannot sustain predominance. *See Beaton v. SpeedyPC Software*, 907 F.3d 1018, 1027–29 (7th Cir. 2018) (affirming denial of certification where individualized questions about class members' circumstances predominated); *Oshana v. Coca-Cola Co.*, 472 F.3d 506, 513–15 (7th Cir. 2006) (affirming denial of certification where individualized questions of injury and causation foreclosed predominance).

### C. Individualized Injury Questions Compound the Problem.

The damages inquiry here cannot be separated from the question of injury. A class defined to include members who suffered no harm, or whose harm cannot be identified without individualized inquiry, cannot satisfy predominance. *Oshana*, 472 F.3d at 514; *see also Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 757–61 (7th Cir. 2014) (reversing certification where individualized issues, including whether each purchaser was deceived and harmed, predominated). Because the same individualized evidence that determines whether a member was injured also determines the amount of that injury, the damages questions cannot be deferred without rendering the common questions largely academic.

### D. Rule 23(c)(4) and Bifurcation Do Not Cure the Defect.

Plaintiffs may invoke *Butler* to urge issue certification or a separate damages phase. But *Butler* reflects a discretionary tool for cases in which classwide resolution of liability issues will materially advance the litigation. 727 F.3d at 800–02. It does not permit certification of an otherwise unmanageable case. Resolving the common questions here would leave every contested element of each member's claim for individual adjudication. That would not advance the litigation and would only postpone the inevitable fragmentation. *See Saltzman v. Pella Corp.*, 606 F.3d 391, 394–96 (7th Cir. 2010) (vacating certification where the common issues did not justify aggregate treatment of individualized claims).

### E. Conclusion

Because individualized damages and injury questions, not common ones, will consume the litigation, Plaintiffs cannot satisfy Rule 23(b)(3)'s predominance requirement. The class certification order should be [reversed/affirmed in denying certification].
